hero.title: Guiding the next generation of FIRST.
hero.subtitle: Every GEarheads member started in FIRST LEGO League. Now we judge FLL events, bring our FTC robot to show what's next, give talks on making the jump to FTC, and help parents start teams of their own.

impact.label: Why it matters
impact.text: We started as FLL kids ourselves — building robots on a cafeteria table before qualifying for the FTC World Championship. When we show up at an FLL event, we're not outside visitors. We're proof of where it can lead, and that carries more weight than any pitch.

approach.label: Our Approach
approach.heading: We were those kids. Now we show them the path.
approach.body:
The best thing we can offer FLL students is proof, not a pitch: real students, a few years older, who walked into their first FLL meeting clueless and came out at a World Championship. "We were doing exactly this a few years ago" lands harder than any recruiting speech.

We show up a few ways: judging projects and robot runs, bringing our FTC robot for kids to see and drive, and giving keynotes to parents and students together.

Parent guidance gets extra attention because most outreach skips it. Parents want their kid to stay in FIRST but don't know what starting an FTC team really costs or takes — so we just tell them straight.

activities.label: Judging FLL Projects
activities.tagline: Reading research projects alongside certified FLL judges.
activities.description: Certified judges lead each panel, and our members sit alongside them scoring Innovation Projects and Core Values demonstrations. It goes both ways — we see exactly what judges look for, and teams get feedback from people who did this a few years ago. Reading dozens of notebooks in a day also makes the gap between a strong one and a thin one obvious, which sharpens how we write our own afterward.
highlights: Sit alongside certified FLL judges in project review
Score Innovation Projects and Core Values demos
Give feedback from a near-peer perspective
See firsthand what FLL judging standards require
Bring it back into our own notebook and portfolio work

activities.label: FTC Robot Showcase
activities.tagline: A working FTC robot on the FLL event floor — driven by students, for students.
activities.description: We bring our full competition robot to FLL events, set it up for live demos, and let kids drive it when the schedule allows — explaining each part plainly, including designs that didn't work and why. Seeing a machine built by 13-to-18-year-olds answers the question every FLL family is quietly asking: what does this lead to? We've had students spend twenty minutes asking mechanism questions, and parents ask afterward how their kid could join a team like ours.
highlights: Full FTC competition robot at the event
Live driving demos and hands-on interaction when possible
Plain-language rundown of subsystems and design decisions
Honest talk about what failed and what we learned
A tangible answer to 'what does FLL lead to?'

activities.label: FLL → FTC Keynote
activities.tagline: Sharing the GEarheads FLL-to-FTC journey, unfiltered.
activities.description: We tell our own story straight — what our first FLL season felt like, why we started an FTC team, what we had to figure out. Not a recruiting pitch, just an honest account, including the hard parts: fundraising, finding a mentor, a workspace, harder robots. We pair the real costs with the moments that made it worth it. Parents have told us it's the first time FTC felt real instead of aspirational.
highlights: Our real FLL-to-FTC origin story, unfiltered
A clear picture of what FTC is and how it differs
Honest talk on commitment, costs, and challenges
The moments that made it worth it
Q&A with students and parents together

activities.label: Parent Guidance
activities.tagline: Demystifying the FTC transition for the families who drive it.
activities.description: Kids rarely make the jump to FTC alone — they need a parent who understands what it takes. So we talk with FLL parents directly about season logistics, realistic costs, finding a mentor or sponsor, and what Wisconsin's FTC community offers. We also answer what parents are afraid to ask out loud: is my kid technical enough (yes, with the right culture), how much time does this take (more than expected, but it fits around school), and what if we don't qualify (still worth it — most teams improve fast in year two).
highlights: What an FTC season looks like start to finish
Team formation: mentors, sponsors, and workspace
Realistic costs and funding sources
Wisconsin FTC community resources and support
Honest answers to the questions parents hesitate to ask
